commits.subject: Vibe Francisco: two hundred cars, fifteen boats, and a Ferry Building that fits
commits.lede: A city with nothing moving in it reads as a model of a city. You notice immediately and cannot say why — the buildings are right, the streets are right, the hills are right, and the whole thing still looks like something under glass. So: cars on the grid and boats on the bay, two instanced meshes between them.

commits.subject: Vibe Francisco: land on a street, and a camera that flies itself
commits.lede: Spawns snap to the nearest asphalt. They are stored as the real lat/lon of a real place, which is right, and lands you wherever that place falls relative to a generated street grid — for Fisherman's Wharf that was the middle of a block, in a courtyard between the backs of four buildings with no way out, which reads as a bug in the collision system rather than as a spawn point. A spiral search puts every one of them o

commits.subject: Vibe Francisco: a logbook, a hundred and seventy coins, and a race up Market
commits.lede: Three reasons to go somewhere, in one new file.

commits.subject: Vibe Francisco gets its landmarks, and the city gets its walls back
commits.lede: Twelve buildings, hand-made from the real ones: the Transamerica Pyramid, Salesforce Tower, Coit Tower, the Ferry Building, Grace Cathedral, the Dragon Gate, the Dewey Monument on Union Square, Pier 39, the crooked block of Lombard Street, the Powell Street cable car turnaround, the Bay Bridge, and Alcatraz. They are the only things in the world that get the cartoon outline, because an outline on everything is an out

commits.subject: The water soundscape, and an ending nobody had ever reached
commits.lede: THE FINDING: the victory path had never executed once. Not broken — DRAIN_CURVE holds the lobby at 100 for eighteen seconds and only reaches one survivor at t=820 simulated seconds, a fourteen-minute match at 60 fps and about a day and a half under SwiftSHADER. That is why neither end card had ever been seen. match.skipToEnd() makes the ending reachable the way skipToLive made the ground reachable, and it deliberatel

commits.subject: Vibe Francisco: a toy San Francisco you can fly around
commits.lede: A new world at /frisco — downtown San Francisco built as painted wood rather than photographed concrete. Two street grids meeting at Market, the hills in the right order, the bay on two sides, and eleven districts that read as themselves from the air: Chinatown red and gold, the Financial District glass and slate, North Beach in pastels.

commits.subject: Put the city on a beat, and made a crowd sound like one
commits.lede: The dances were already the most tightly synchronised thing in the world and the least perceptible. Every character runs off `Date.now()` at one tempo, so two people who start the same move ten seconds apart are genuinely in step — and in silence that reads as coincidence rather than as anything happening. So: music, on the same clock.

commits.subject: Stamp dates for the worlds that arrived while this was in flight
commits.lede: Regenerated after rebasing onto the Midnight Zone, Glass Lake, Dune Sea and the letterbox work — npm run stamp reads each world's source, so the dates on the cards were four worlds out of date the moment the rebase landed.

commits.subject: Exploring pays, because nothing else did
commits.lede: The ledger said something bleak. Of 495 wallets, 491 sat at exactly the 100 coins they were handed on arrival, ONE had ever gone past it, and the richest in the whole vibeverse held 116. Three cosmetics had ever been bought, all on one afternoon. `game_reward` had fired once in its life.

commits.subject: A crashed world ended the smoke run green
commits.lede: `npm run smoke` opens all fifty-four routes and is the only automated check that a world still comes up. It has four verdicts: canvas, text, blank, and crash — the last one when the route renders the app's own crash screen, which is deliberately the WORST outcome, because a blank route might still be loading while a crashed one has already given up.

commits.subject: ✉️ The paper takes letters, and Vibey finally reads it out loud
commits.lede: Two things the paper was missing: a way in, and a voice.

commits.subject: The bay has something in it, and you can finally look up
commits.lede: The sea got waves, then a floor, then caustics on the floor, then fish over the caustics, then a way to swim down through all of it — and no reason to. You dive once, see the best-looking thing in the world, surface, and never dive again. Three commits of ocean making a very good set and not a place.

commits.subject: Everybody starts as a mushroom
commits.lede: The default character was Vibey, the fallback for an unknown id was Flux, and Webslinger sat at index 1 — so the second face anybody saw in the vibeverse was a wall-crawler, in every picker, on every surface that lists the roster. It is Toadstool now: the default, the fallback, and the first tile.

commits.subject: 🔦 The Midnight Zone was unplayable, and none of it showed up in a build
commits.lede: Jack played the thing I shipped and got a black screen most of the time, a descent that never ended, and something he described as very glitchy. All of it was real, all of it was mine, and every single one got past a green build, a green typecheck, 1,528 passing tests and a set of screenshots I took myself.

commits.subject: A card for San Francisco that shows the city it is now
commits.lede: The old one predated the walking mode, the ten landmarks and the lighting work. Captured from the running world at golden hour off Telegraph Hill, looking down Columbus into the Financial District — Coit Tower, Washington Square, North Beach's roofs, the Transamerica and the Salesforce spike and the bay, in one frame.

commits.subject: Traffic can knock you over, water muffles the world, and /city got measured
commits.lede: Three things, and the third one found a regression I had shipped.

commits.subject: sf-flicker was measuring a falling character
commits.lede: /sf opens in walking mode now, and `setPose` moves the PLAYER rather than a detached camera. So the probe's own poses — 236 m over the Financial District, 22 m above Market Street — handed the walking controller a character in mid-air, and it did the correct thing with it: dropped it. The settle test is defined as two frames of a frozen pose. It was comparing two frames of a fall, reading 37%, and blaming the city.

commits.lede: The glitching was one bug, and it was not the one it looked like. A chunk that generates no geometry — water, park, the Presidio's meadows, a third of this map — was treated as "not built yet" rather than "built, and empty", so every rescan rebuilt every one of them, four hundred milliseconds apart, forever. The queue never drained in a whole session, real chunks queued behind work already done, and the LOD cross-fad

commits.lede: The world looked flat, washed out and wrong, and it was not the lighting. The terrain mesh's triangle winding was inverted, so three culled every face that pointed at the camera. What rendered was the handful of slopes angled *away* — the rest of the frame was the sky dome showing straight through the floor. It reads exactly like an overexposed desert, which is why it survived four passes at the shading: every one of

commits.subject: Drive into the sea and the sea does something about it
commits.lede: `CollisionWorld` floors everything at y=0 so nothing can fall out of the world, and over open water that floor is a phantom plate with no mesh under it. Every ground query a car made therefore answered "sea level, go ahead" — so a kart driven off the quay carried on driving, at sea level, across the bay, wheels spinning on nothing. With an ocean this good it was the loudest remaining tell that the water is scenery.

commits.lede: A new world at /glass-lake. It is night, you are on a hundred and ninety metres of frozen lake, and the sky above it is not a texture.

commits.subject: The sea has an inside now: dive under Vibe City
commits.lede: The ocean had a top and nothing behind it. You could swim on it, and the moment your eyes went under, the world carried on being the world — same fog, same sky, same flat blue sheet seen from a side it was never drawn for. This is the other half, reached by aiming the camera down and swimming.

commits.subject: A world was added and three homepages said fifty-three anyway
commits.lede: The Midnight Zone landed on main, and Aurora, Swiss and Storybook each went on announcing "Fifty-three worlds" over a grid of fifty-four — because each of them had spelled the number out by hand in its headline. That is exactly the failure `registry.ts` was built to end, reappearing in a new directory.

commits.subject: Step through the fifteen with a key, and fix Riso's smear
commits.lede: `[` and `]` walk the bake-off. Not the arrow keys: Console drives its shelves with those, so a stepper bound to them would step the theme and scroll the shelf on the same press. Verified both — `]]]` walks midnight→alpine→editorial→zine, and two ArrowRights inside Console move its cursor and leave the URL alone.

commits.subject: 🔦 THE MIDNIGHT ZONE: eight kilometres straight down, and the light runs out
commits.lede: Forty-four worlds in the vibeverse and not one of them underwater. So: a submersible, trimmed slightly heavy so it sinks on its own, and 8,200 m of ocean between you and the floor of the trench.

commits.subject: Zine put its wall below the fold, which is the only thing Zine is
commits.lede: The headline was set to 12vw and stacked above the collage, so the first screen of a theme whose entire argument is "worlds pinned to a wall at angles" was a sentence on black. The text now sits beside the wall and sticks while it scrolls, which is also more like an actual zine — the writing pinned up among the pictures rather than introducing them.

commits.subject: Alpine lost its sign-in button on a phone, and nothing noticed
commits.lede: The nav did not wrap, so at 390px the last item ran off the edge of the sky — which has `overflow: hidden`, so the page did not scroll, nothing was reported, and the button was simply gone. Every check passed on a homepage you could not sign in from.

commits.subject: The picker shows you the page, not a paragraph about the page
commits.lede: `/homes` listed fifteen candidates as three-colour swatches and a sentence each, which is enough to tell them apart and not nearly enough to choose between them. It now carries a live preview beside the list: hover a row, see that homepage running.

commits.subject: Ten more front doors, and every one of them argues with the rest
commits.lede: Completes the bake-off at `/homes`. The ten added here are structural rather than tonal — the point of fifteen is lost the moment two of them are the same layout in different colours:

commits.subject: Fifteen front doors, and a way to walk through them — first five
commits.lede: `/homes` is a bake-off. Each candidate is a whole page — its own layout, type, palette and card — not a skin over one design, because fifteen token-swaps of the same page tell you nothing a swatch could not. The variety has to be structural or the exercise is theatre.

commits.subject: Stamped the royale cards with the teammate's date
commits.lede: `npm run stamp` on this machine rewrites every timestamp from +00:00 to Z, which is 500 lines of churn and no information, so this is the two entries that actually changed.

commits.subject: The teammate stopped standing in a field, and started keeping score
commits.lede: It played one life. Soaked out at 0% meant standing still until somebody killed the process — through the end card, through the next lobby, through the next match. One session sat in an empty field for eleven hours. And it learned nothing: every match started the beginner it was the first time.

commits.subject: Measured what the worlds cost, and stopped guessing which models are rigged
commits.lede: `route-smoke.mjs` answers "is the world there". Nothing answered "and what does it cost", so `npm run perf` now does: draw calls, triangles, shader programs, texture bytes, live GL contexts and JS heap, per route. It counts at the WebGL layer rather than through renderer.info, because forty-odd worlds build their renderer in forty-odd places and most never expose it.

commits.subject: Every day of the vibeverse, one square each
commits.lede: The Chronicle told you what was built. It could not tell you what the building looked like — and the shape of the work turns out to be the better story.

commits.subject: Real cars in Vibe City, and you can walk into them
commits.lede: The traffic was `BoxGeometry(1.8, 1.25, 4.2)` sliding along the street centrelines at a constant speed. No wheels, no lights, no collision, and cross traffic drove straight through itself at every junction. The comment defending it was honest — from any altitude where you can see the grid, you cannot see that nobody is turning — and it stopped being true the moment anybody stood on the pavement.

commits.subject: Fixed the swim stroke lurching, and made it a real crawl
commits.lede: The stroke was being re-randomised every frame, and nothing about the pose was to blame.

commits.subject: Your own line in the history
commits.lede: The Chronicle tells the vibeverse's story and had nothing to say about yours. The passport does, and it is the only page that can: it knows the earliest arrival in this browser, `REPO_LIFE` knows the first commit there ever was, and the difference between them is a fact nothing else here could produce — not when you turned up, but how far into the story.

commits.subject: Build log catches up with the Chronicle
commits.lede: Regenerated by `prebuild` on the last build, so it now carries the Chronicle and the merge rather than stopping short of them. Generated artifact — the churn is a timestamp and the newest commits, nothing to read.

commits.subject: The Chronicle learns its own birthday
commits.lede: `npm run stamp && npm run chronicle`, now that the page has a commit to read. It is the fifty-third world and the newest line in its own history: born 2026-08-14, one commit, one hand.

commits.subject: The Chronicle: every world, in the order it appeared
commits.lede: The vibeverse has fifty-two worlds and no memory of building any of them. `/game` shows what exists and the passport shows where you have been; nothing has ever shown how the place came to be. This is that — and it writes itself, out of git, so it is exactly as true as the repository and cannot drift from it. Add a world and it writes itself a line here.

commits.subject: Build log catches up with the last two commits
commits.lede: Regenerated by the build, so it now carries the chrome default and the motion-card work rather than stopping two commits short of them.

commits.subject: Chrome is the front door now, and five more to try
commits.lede: `DEFAULT_LOOK` moves to chrome, so a first-time visitor with nothing saved gets the brushed-metal wordmark instead of the mint one. Checked with a clean profile rather than assumed: no localStorage, and the h1 comes up with a transparent fill and the gradient behind it.

commits.subject: Seven cards play, and the list is a result rather than a choice
commits.lede: "Every game, or the top ten?" turned out to be the wrong question — most worlds physically cannot be recorded, so which cards move is discovered, not decided. Fourteen worlds have a `?shot` mode; seven of them move on their own.

commits.subject: The recorder judges its own output
commits.lede: Pointing the GIF recorder at a list of worlds is only safe if it can tell when it has filmed nothing. "A world that waits at a title screen records a title screen" was a line in a comment, which is the kind of warning nobody remembers to act on at the moment it matters.

commits.subject: Seafair and Vibe Star get the card art they were missing
commits.lede: Seafair is a flagship in the README and was showing the drawn fallback panel, which is the one card on the grid where that reads as an oversight rather than a choice. Both captures are real frames from the running worlds.

commits.subject: Six ways the front door could look, and a page to pick one
commits.lede: The headline has been mint green since the first commit — which is the accent the play *currency* uses everywhere else, so the loudest type on the site was quietly saying "coins" rather than "vibeverse". Jack asked for white, and for options rather than one guess.

commits.subject: COIL's card plays COIL
commits.lede: A screenshot of a game is a picture of a game not being played. It shows the art and hides the only thing anybody wants to know, which is what it feels like to move in there. COIL's card is three seconds of the real thing now — no editing, no capture card, no human. The world plays itself and we film it.

commits.subject: Two coins, told apart on the front door — and the token's market cap
commits.lede: **The market cap, top right.** `$VIBE $70.78K ▼4.2%`, next to the play balance. A number that moves is the cheapest possible proof that the token half of this is not a metaphor, and until now the only page that knew the price was the wallet.

commits.subject: A fresh clone could not install, so none of the checks could run
commits.lede: `postprocessing` was declared `^6.35.0` and resolved to 6.39, which is the release that raised its floor to `three >= 0.168`. Three is pinned at 0.160 here and moving it is a day of work in forty worlds, so npm called the tree impossible and installed nothing at all — no node_modules, and therefore no typecheck, no build, no test, no smoke. Every check CLAUDE.md asks for before pushing to a live `main` was unavailabl

commits.subject: Vibe Island stopped opening if your character had no model file
commits.lede: Anyone whose saved character was one of the code-built ones — Flux and the two dozen others in `src/lib/characters.ts` with an empty `url` — opened /city and got the crash screen. The report was "whenever I try to open Vibe Island it says a corner of the Vibeverse glitched", and `client_errors` had been saying `Cannot access 'headMount' before initialization` since 16:18 that afternoon.

commits.subject: Work in progress
The form fills itself in while you type
commits.lede: Pasting a link was a leap of faith: you pressed Submit and only then found out what we had decided your game was called. Now the card fills in underneath the field, which is the same information a beat earlier and the difference between a form and a conversation.

commits.subject: Hats that are actually on the head, and three more of them
commits.lede: Hats were parented to the model holder at a fixed 1.78 m — "just above a ~1.85 m model's head" — which is true of a character standing still and of nothing else. Every character in the catalogue is a different GLB fitted to the same overall height, so their heads sit at different places inside it: the same number floats over a short one and cuts through a tall one. And because the mount never moved, the hat stayed bo

commits.subject: The city's controls fit on one row
commits.lede: Ten chips wanting 752px, and the strip holding them was never wider than half the screen — so three rows at 900px and two at 1440px.

commits.subject: Swimming, and snow that settles
commits.lede: Two things you could see the world wanting the moment it had a beach.

commits.subject: Vibe Island stops showing you somebody else's screen first
commits.lede: Clicking Vibe Island painted the character picker for a beat, then a loading screen, then the island. Same for Powder Peak, the moon, Mars, TJ's, Vibestar and the mines — half the world list is a `/city?spawn=…` link, so this was most of what "going to a world" looked like.

commits.subject: The avatar is the character's actual face
commits.lede: The chip in the corner has always shown an emoji — 🤖 for Vibey, 🦀 for Pinch — which identifies a species rather than a character. Sixty-three characters are built from one rig and photographed from it, so the corner can show the one you picked.

commits.subject: Submit a game without leaving the shelf
commits.lede: "Add yours →" and "Put your game here" both sent you to `/build`, which is a page about the deal rather than the form — so acting on the invitation meant two navigations away from the thing that made you want to. The arcade shelf is the argument for submitting; a form on its own route has to make that argument again from scratch.

commits.subject: Powered by creators, owned by players
commits.lede: The old arcade's line, back above the wordmark. "Every builder grows the universe" said one half of it — anybody can add a door — and stopped there. This one says the other half too: what you earn behind the door is yours. It is the claim /manifesto spends a page on ("Build worlds. Share ownership. Play forever.") in six words, in the slot a tagline goes.

The render is the real artwork and it paints in one frame off the image cache; the object turns, catches the light differently every second, and can react to things — and costs three.js, a GLB and a WebGL context to say so.

commits.subject: The boss's shard was a white plate, not a gem
commits.lede: At 2.4× scale an additive white icosahedron at 0.95 opacity blows out into a flat slab the size of the boss's head. Smaller, amber, dimmer, and turning — a piece of God Orb it is carrying rather than a hole in the render.

commits.lede: Editing a source file while the probe is up sends vite's hot reload through page.evaluate, which throws "execution context was destroyed" and killed the run seconds before its summary. One skipped sample is the right response.

commits.subject: 254 MB of models becomes 70 MB, and nothing looks different
commits.lede: None of the .glb files in this repo had ever been through an optimiser. floating-island.glb was 38.7 MB and 1,049,034 triangles — for a decorative island that renders about 300 px wide behind a menu. That is a frame-rate problem on every phone that opens the hub before it is a download problem, and it is simply what a Meshy export looks like when nobody runs the last step.

commits.subject: Gave everybody in the city a body that can actually dance
commits.lede: The emote wheel could throw an emoji over your head, which is a label for a feeling rather than a performance of it: press 💃 and a pink sprite bobs above a character standing perfectly still. Nobody was dancing. Now T picks a move at random and the body does it — and pressing T again picks a different one.

commits.subject: Vibe Island: gave the keel something to be
commits.lede: From the city, Vibe Island resolved to a green disc on a smooth beige wedge — and the wedge is the half of a floating island that says "floating" rather than "hill". It was the last flat thing left.

commits.subject: Restamped Vibe Island
commits.lede: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com> Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KSa7cEFu3r5gZdH7gNjnBz

commits.subject: Vibe Island: a real tree, a real pool, and a lawn worth standing in
commits.lede: Follow-up to the grass pass, all of it the same argument — the thing your eye lands on is whichever object in frame is still made of one flat value.

commits.subject: Stopped the city shimmering when you look at it from the air
commits.lede: Vibe City's ground is a stack of near-coplanar surfaces: the asphalt plate at y=0, the sidewalks 1.2 cm above it, the crossings 2 cm above those, and now the beach running a few metres underneath the plate's edge. On the street those are real gaps. From six hundred metres up they are no gap at all.

commits.subject: Restamped Vibe Island
commits.lede: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com> Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KSa7cEFu3r5gZdH7gNjnBz

commits.subject: Gave Vibe Island real grass, and real cardboard
commits.lede: The lawn was a 1024px canvas stretched over a 110 m disc — about nine pixels per metre — so standing on the island put you on a flat mint plane with a path painted on it. No redraw of that canvas fixes it; at ankle height there was nothing there to see.

commits.subject: Sign in with MetaMask, and finish wiring Google
commits.lede: Both buttons under the divider in the sign-in dialog said "soon" and popped a toast saying so. Now they sign you in, and they land in the same place every other door does — a Supabase session — so no world has to know which one somebody used.

commits.subject: Fourteen characters that are not a person in a costume
commits.lede: Every code-built character before this one was, underneath the paint, the same body: two legs, two arms, a head on top. Twenty side by side read as twenty costumes, and the design table says why in as many words — silhouette is what a player recognises, and silhouette is mostly how a thing moves. So these are three new body plans first and fourteen designs second.
